parameter_provenance.basis: ATB2024 Commercial Battery Storage models 1–8 h durations and uses a four-hour system for its base-year cost illustration. Four hours is a reference-informed research candidate, not an identified optimum for this AIDC.

parameter_provenance.value: 1 MW PCC-referred AC / 4 MWh internal stored energy
parameter_provenance.basis: Preserve user-selected 1 MW PCC-referred AC power and 4 MWh internal energy from v2. No sizing change in v3. P_AC/E_internal=0.25 h^-1 is a nominal system ratio, not an electrochemical cell C-rate.

User chose 90% for each effective PCC-referred charge and discharge efficiency. This gives 81% round-trip efficiency, NOT 90% or the previously adopted ATB 85%. Rounded research scenario, not a universal battery value. No additional UPS/inverter/transformer efficiency is applied to ESS flows.
SOC window is not claimed to be an ATB default or universal battery standard. PL6 Eq23/24 supports SOC accounting, mutually exclusive ports and cyclic endpoint structure, not these numerical values.

parameter_provenance.parameter: ESS standing loss and dedicated auxiliaries
parameter_provenance.basis: No separately calibrated auxiliary consumption, thermal management, self-discharge, degradation or backup reserve. They are not claimed physically zero. RTE aggregates conversion/cycling loss only; omitted time-dependent losses should be revisited for deployment.
Inherited candidate retains PL30/REopt provenance. Disabled TES means device absent, no standby charge. Comparisons across hardware portfolios are not equal-investment comparisons.

references.title: 2024 Annual Technology Baseline: Commercial Battery Storage
references.used: Duration-range and four-hour scenario context only for v3. ATB representative 85% RTE described the previous v2 baseline; current 81% RTE is a user-selected assumption.

references.title: Data center load modeling through optimal energy consumption characteristics: A path to simultaneously enhance energy efficiency and demand response quality
references.used: PDF p9 Eq23, pp10–11 Eq24: stored energy, power bounds, exclusive ports, no export and initial/final state constraints. Original UPS backup capacity and 0.98/0.96 efficiency are not used.

scope: Dedicated dispatch ESS is separate from existing UPS; no assumption that emergency backup capacity is available for demand management.

ESS electrical ports are referred to the PCC AC boundary, with effective end-to-end efficiencies. Battery and conversion losses are assumed outside the modeled server-room thermal boundary; existing IT cooling input remains frozen.
Both storage devices can charge or discharge independently, but neither device can charge and discharge simultaneously. No predetermined ESS-fast/TES-slow roles in a 5-minute model.
Hypothetical 5-minute mean PCC caps; perfect-foresight offline optimization, not DSO-derived DOE, tariff optimization, uncertain forecasting, rolling control, DFL or HIL.
ESS-only excludes TES and its standby losses. Joint/TES-only keep the identical TES; all enabled devices end at their starting SOC. Joint adds hardware, not an equal-budget comparison.

Four-hour E/P is a nominal ratio, not guaranteed four-hour AC discharge. SOC90–10 gives3.2MWh internal usable energy and2.88MWh AC delivery at eta_dis=.9, or2.88h at1MW. InitialSOC50% gives1.44h without precharge. Initial/terminal internalenergy2MWh.

Only ESS charge and discharge efficiencies change from sqrt(.85) to.9. Same1MW/4MWh, sameSOC endpoints, sameTES and caps. Compare with v2; lowering efficiency is not assumed to preserve feasibility or improve objective.
